subject: How to model individual heterogeneity and sex differences in capture probability

messages.author: b0621462f80cbf25
messages.subject: How to model individual heterogeneity and sex differences in capture probability
parts:
Hello, 
I am using SECR in R to model the density of a chimpanzee community, based on capture recapture data from camera traps.  I would like to imodel three covariates and their combinations,  sex, age (which is just adult or juvenile) and individual heterogeneity in capture probability and compare them with AIC to see which fits best.   So I will have

null model
sex
age
individual
age + sex, 
sex + individual
age + individual
age + sex + individual

I have modeled sex differences with a hybrid mixture model, as we do not know the sexes of all individuals caught in the cameras, using the following code, which I can also get the age differences from (ages are only recorded as juvenile or adult).

secr.sex<-secr.fit(myCH1, hcov = "sex", mask = maskXY, trace = FALSE)

and I tried modelling just individual heterogeneity (following the chapter in the SECR book) with 

secr.ind<-secr.fit(myCH1, model = list(D~1, g0~h2, sigma~h2), mask = maskXY, trace = FALSE, CL= TRUE)

however i do not get a density estimate in the output of this model and I do not know how to create combinations of these.  So if someone could kindly advise me on how to:

1. model individual heterogeneity so i get a density estimate
2. create the models with the combinations of these factors, 

I would be most appreciative

Thanks
Alex

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: How to model individual heterogeneity and sex differences in capture probability
parts:
Hello Alex

 

I take a fairly jaundiced view of attempts to construct intricate models of the detection parameters in SECR models, especially when the data are limited, so I may not be the best person to respond. However, I can clarify a couple of points that may help get you moving.

 

The hybrid mixture approach that allows for both known- and unknown-sex individuals co-opts (takes over) the finite-mixture variable 'h2'. This has two consequences

 

(1) to fit a sex-specific hybrid mixture model you _both_ define the individual covariate for class membership where known (hcov = 'sex') _and_ specify 'h2' in the formula:

secr.sex<-secr.fit(myCH1, model = list(g0~h2, sigma~h2), hcov = "sex", mask = maskXY)

This can be compared by AIC with

secr.null<-secr.fit(myCH1, hcov = "sex", mask = maskXY)

[note the need to define hcov for both]

 

(2) Having used h2 in this way, there is no way in 'secr' to model additional ('unmodelled') individual variation - the usual understanding of h2.

 

When CL = TRUE, secr.fit fits only the detection parameters (g0, sigma). The term for D in your model will be ignored. You can estimate D as a derived parameter , using the 'secr' function 'derived': derived(secr.ind)

 

It can happen that bias in density estimates due to ignoring sources of heterogeneity in detection is a minor component of error in the density estimates. Also, finite mixture models (h2 without hcov) are prone to problems during fitting, so take a deep breath and master other aspects before you go there.

 

Another gratuitous comment:  I am curious how you are identifying individuals; it is a bit surprising to me that you may know their identity (and be able to recognise them whenever you see them again), but not their sex.

 


Murray

messages.author: 0dbfcf0efe4ff8fe
messages.subject: Re: How to model individual heterogeneity and sex differences in capture probability
parts:
Alex, it may also be worth mentioning that AIC values from models fit using the full likelihood (CL = FALSE; the default) aren't comparable to those from models fit where CL = TRUE.  If you want to evaluate support for different detection models, generate model averaged estimates, etc, you need to choose either the full or conditional likelihood for all the models.  You need the full likelihood to include covariates of density.

Eric

Good point.

For Alex's benefit, I also point out that Eric has argued in print in an opposite direction to my earlier post: a priori we do expect there to be heterogeneity, which might be an argument for always using finite mixtures. I think the jury is out...

Murray
